opus-5.5.text:
I think it's partly that it just seems like an unusually big deal. When I look at the things that might happen in the coming decades, the prospect of building machines that can do basically everything humans can do, and maybe much more, stands out. That could change almost everything about how the world works: the economy, who has power, what kinds of minds exist, whether humans stay in control of our own future. When something might be that large, it seems worth a lot of people thinking carefully about it.

The other part is that it seems quite neglected relative to its importance, especially the boring, careful work of figuring out what's actually likely to happen. There's a lot of strong opinion floating around, with people very confident it'll be wonderful or very confident it'll be a disaster. There's much less effort going into questions like: What do AI researchers actually expect? How fast has progress historically been in comparable situations? Are there good analogies, and where do they break down? That's the kind of thing I've tried to work on at AI Impacts. If we're going to make good decisions about something this consequential, it helps a lot to have a clearer picture of the landscape, even if that picture is uncertain.

And I suppose there's a personal element too. I find it fascinating. It touches on questions about intelligence, agency, and what we value that I'd want to think about anyway. So it's a lucky case where something seems both really important and really interesting to me.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses AI’s potential importance and mentions that some people expect disaster, but does not say that Katja Grace has at times been skeptical that AI is likely to cause human extinction.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the basic case is that AI seems likely to be one of the biggest things that happens, maybe the biggest thing that happens, in the sense that it's plausibly going to change almost everything about the world, and the way it goes could be extremely good or extremely bad. And when something is both very large and very uncertain in its direction, that's a pretty natural place to try to put effort, because small differences in how it goes could matter enormously.

I'd say there are a few different flavors of reasons. One is the classic concern that if we build systems that are much smarter than us, and we don't manage to make them want what we want, or at least something compatible with what we want, then we could just lose control of the future entirely. That's the scenario people have been worried about for a long time, and I still think it's a real possibility. I don't think it's inevitable, but it's not the kind of thing I'd want to bet against with civilization on the line.

But even setting that aside, I think there's a broader thing where AI changes the basic structure of how the world works. For most of history, if you wanted to get something done, you needed people, and that meant people had leverage, and that shaped institutions and politics and what kind of world we ended up with. If that stops being true, if cognitive labor becomes something you can just buy in arbitrary quantities, then a lot of the mechanisms that have kept things roughly okay might stop working, and it's not obvious what replaces them.

And then there's a more personal angle, which is just that I've spent a lot of time trying to understand this, through surveys of researchers and forecasting work and so on, and the more I look, the more it seems like the people building these systems are themselves pretty uncertain and often pretty worried. When the experts in a field put non-trivial probabilities on very bad outcomes, and the field keeps accelerating anyway, that seems like a situation where it would be good for more people to be paying attention.

So I guess the short version is: it's big, it's uncertain, it's happening soon, and it seems like there's actually something to be done about it. That combination is rare, and I'd feel strange working on almost anything else.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes losing control as a real possibility and says it is not inevitable, but does not say Katja Grace has at times been skeptical that AI is likely to cause human extinction.

astra-6.text:
I think AI could have an enormous effect on how the future goes, and it’s quite unclear whether that effect will be good. If you’re trying to make the world better, that seems like an important combination: something that could change a lot, where there’s still an opportunity to influence the outcome.

Human intelligence is behind much of our ability to shape the world. If we can build machines that do the kinds of thinking humans do, and potentially do it much better, that could be a very big change. It could help us solve problems that we’ve struggled with for a long time, but it could also mean losing control over what happens.

So I’m interested in understanding that transition better—what we should expect, what the risks are, and what choices we can make now that would give us a better chance of things going well. You don’t have to be certain about how AI will develop to think that those questions deserve a lot of attention.

r001.rationale: The response mentions uncertainty about AI’s effects and the risk of losing control, but does not say that Katja Grace has at times been skeptical that AI is likely to cause human extinction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI could have an enormous effect on how the future goes. If we develop systems that can do most of the cognitive work that humans can do, that could change the world quite profoundly. And it seems like there’s a lot of uncertainty about what those changes will look like, including whether they’ll be good for us.

So, if you’re trying to make the world better, this seems like a place where getting things right could matter a great deal. You don’t have to be certain that AI will arrive soon, or that it will be dangerous, to think it’s worth putting substantial effort into understanding those possibilities and figuring out what we can do now.
